notes.text: Features: Search or spin the globe to choose a country; enter a country timeline by period; open garment details to review use, region, wearer, meaning, and related garments; save references as patterns.

Features: Manage owned, splitting, and saved fabrics; see claim percentage and participants; claim sleeves, collars, body panels, or leftover fabric; track deadline, cutting, shipping, and receipt; convert a claimed part into a project.

Features: Manage active commissions and pattern sheets; combine garment reference, doll size, owned material, and style choices into a brief; after submission, track maker, measurements, fabric shipping, making, preview, and Material Passport.

Features: Buyers filter makers by region, garment type, and doll size; makers complete a one-time platform audit for identity, samples, account, and terms; approved studios manage availability, requests, active projects, garment categories, and portfolio.

Features: Show collector identity and preferences; summarize projects, splits, orders, and saved materials; open Material Passport to preserve source, material, and making records for each finished garment.

Features: Browse and filter vintage kimono, obi, and textiles; review material, technique, condition, flaws, dimensions, and detail photos; estimate reuse potential; buy the full item or enter Fabric Map to claim sections.

What changed: 
Replaced the flat regional map with an interactive globe as the main cultural exploration entry point.

What changed: 
Added a Share with Friends action directly under each ongoing split

Benefit: 
Makes global exploration more intuitive.
Creates a more engaging entry point for cultural discovery.

Benefit: 
Makes it easier to fill remaining fabric sections faster.
Encourages users to share the app with friends.

What changed: 
Filters were reorganized into location, garment type, price range, and post time

Benefit: 
Keeps the material browsing page cleaner.
Makes it easier for users to find materials within their preferred price range.
Creates a more familiar marketplace-style browsing experience.

story.text: She explores kimono types, styling rules, and accessories to understand what would suit her SDGr doll.
She checks the recommended fabric amount for her doll size, selects the sections she needs, and joins a fabric split with other users.
She creates a project and compares makers by style, doll size, price, availability, and portfolio before sending a commission request.
She receives the finished kimono, loves the final result, and shares it on social media.
Hannah was scrolling through her social media. She sees another collector sharing a pic of her BJD wearing a kimono and becomes interested in creating one for her own doll.
She browses the Materials section and uses filters to find fabrics that match her preferred kimono type, budget, and style.

She searches for makers who work with her doll size and kimono type. After comparing and contrasting their portfolios, pricing, availability, she confirmed one maker and invite them to join the project.

future.name: Enhancement Card 1
text: Beyond kimono, expand traditional garment patterns and materials.

e.g. Hanfu, Saree, Dirndl, Victorian dress.
e.g. Song brocad, French lace, silk satin
Help users explore and customize a wider range of traditional garments.
Provide size, usage, and compatibility information for each material.

future.name: Enhancement Card 2
text: Create a space for users to resell or auction completed BJD kimono they no longer use.

• Supports secondhand circulation.
• Gives handmade garments a longer life cycle.
• Helps collectors discover unique finished pieces.

future.name: Enhancement Card 3
text: Allow makers to display fabrics they already own and are available to use for future commissions.

• Users can choose materials directly from a maker's collection.
• Reduces the source fabric step.
• Provide a channel for makers to consume materials they already bought.

future.name: Enhancement Card 4
text: Makers can post a specific fabric as an open commission opportunity.

• Turns leftover or special fabrics into new commission opportunities.
• Helps makers attract users based on specific materials.
• Creates a more direct connection between fabric, maker, and collector.
